tagline: A progressive's guide to voting in Kansas City, Missouri

title: This Won’t Save Us
subtitle: A Progressive’s Guide to the November 3, 2026 Midterm Election in Kansas City, Missouri

children.text: After a harrowing few months, we’re back to voting in our original legislative districts. And as a treat, the Final Boss of Not Taking No For An Answer, Missouri secretary of state Denny Hoskins, had a
class-action lawsuit filed against him
seeking roughly $80 million dollars for refusing to certify petition signatures. The bad news is that the gerrymandered map will go into effect for future elections if Proposition A passes (vote NO).
We have yet another attack on our access to healthcare in the form of Amendment 3. Only this time around, conservatives know they can’t win on abortion, so they’ve pivoted to attacking trans kids.

But Jesus Christ, how many times are we going to need to vote on the same shit again and again? I know - or at least I hope - that a spectrum of political beliefs find their way to this guide, but I think it’s safe to assume that we share a belief that our democratically elected officials should represent the will of people. That’s why everyone should get behind Amendment 6.
As far as methodology, I’m mostly just googling and going down rabbit holes, but broadly, I’m:

Reviewing campaign funding reports filed with the Federal Election Committee (FEC) and Missouri Ethics Committee (MEC). These tell me who’s funding their campaigns - ideally we’d like to see a mix of individual donors, local organizations, and trustworthy labor unions*.
For judges, I look at the review from their peers at
https://yourmissourijudges.org
. I also create an anonymous survey and solicit opinions from individuals with experience in the courtrooms
Checking federal candidates on
Integrity Index
Reviewing their accomplishments in prior political office or their career. For senators or representatives, I’m seeing which bills they’ve sponsored or co-sponsored.
Reading interviews and listening to candidate forums
Looking for any news articles or even discussions on KC twitter/reddit
Tracking their money from Israel lobbies and their voting record through the
Congressional Democrat Palestine Tracker

*I say trustworthy because not all unions are created equal. I’ve written about this in past guides, but some are using their power, money, and influence to ensure politicians back developments that aren’t in the public interest. I’ll never get this guide out if I try to include it, but I think there’s important research to be done around which unions are corroborating with data centers and backing our local politicians.

This work is researched and written by me, Brynne Musser, but with the guidance of lots of smart people whose opinions and expertise I couldn’t do without - thank you for your patience and generosity. I post all the guides from my personal instagram, @itspurplemink. All the sources I use are linked throughout the document, but keep in mind that there’s simply no citation for a woman’s intuition.
As I’ve said before, this is less a guide than a public documentation of how I’m voting and why. If you think I’m wrong or missed some information, please
email me!
I’ll gladly make an edit.

helpItems.title: Breaking the House and Senate Supermajorities

children.text: For the first time in over a decade, Missouri democrats may be able to overcome the republican supermajorities in the house and the senate. The
dems need to flip
three seats in the House and two in the Senate. Although it’s more useful under a democratic governor,
breaking the republican supermajority
could decrease the speed and volume at which they’re rolling through harmful legislation.
Here are some races with the potential to flip:

links.label: Tracey Steele -  House 12th District (southern Platte County)
Mary Ann Perkins - House 100th District (western St. Louis County)

children.text: At the time of posting this, there are 7 days left to knock doors, make calls, have conversations, or donate. Here are the races and ballot initiatives that need all hands on deck:

There are 435 Representatives in the House, 8 of whom represent Missouri. Representatives serve for two-year terms, so they’re up for election every even year. A good representative should go to Washington DC, write bills, listen to their constituents, whip votes, vote for good stuff and against bad stuff. Of the 8 current Missouri representatives, two are democrats (Cleaver from our 5th District and Wesley Bell from St. Louis’s 1st District) while the other 6 are republicans. Currently republicans control the house with 219 representatives; the democrats have 212, and four seats are vacant (three democrat, one republican).
For what it’s worth, the US Senate currently has 53 republicans*, 45 democrats, and 2 independents (who typically vote with the democrats).
*Including Mitch McConnell’s corpse.
Look, anyone who read the midterm guide knows where I stand on Jordan Herrera. But fortunately for him, he’s running against one of the biggest pieces of shit on the ballot.
I know most of you don’t need to be convinced not to vote for republican incumbent
Mark Alford

, but I need to take a minute to talk about what a piece of shit he really is. In DC, he is the vice chairman of the house appropriations subcommittee on military construction and veterans affairs. His other subcommittees include “commerce, justice, science and related agencies”, “financial services and general government”, and “national security, state and related programs”. He’s co-chair of four caucuses: Broadcasters, Real Estate, Long Range Strike, and Small Business.
Now, keep those committees in mind when you hear
who’s backing his campaign

. His top contributor this election is the pro-genocide lobbying group American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, who’ve donated over $80k. Also in the top contributors are two PACs from weapons manufacturers, Boeing and Northrop Grumman, donated $21k and $18k, respectively. $330k of his campaign donations come from corporate PACs, and 60% of his donors live outside of Missouri!

The vast majority of Missourians, regardless of their party, are tired of US aggression and war, tired of our government giving billions to weapons manufacturers, tired of media we cannot trust, tired of living in a surveillance state, tired of corporations buying our politicians, and tired of politicians that so easily sell out their constituents. This is a rare and special opportunity to build a coalition across Missouri of voters dedicated to GETTING THIS MAN OUT OF CONGRESS!
Thomas Holbrook‘s
website
is a fun read, but he’s not a serious person.
KathleenMae Rogers’ name won’t appear on the ballot, but she’s running as a write-in candidate.
The Issues
page of her website is relatively detailed, and besides being heavy handed in the military funding, I pretty much agree with her on everything.
While I’m glad we’re not in the gerrymandered maps, it pretty much guarantees a win for Alford unless his constituents begin to hold him accountable for his betrayal of the working class.
Because of his
“ironclad support” of Israel,
I’ve abstained from voting for
Emanuel Cleaver

in the last couple elections. On one hand, he has acknowledged the suffering of Palestinians and made some correct decisions; he sponsored a resolution calling for humanitarian aid for Gaza as well as the UNRWA Funding Emergency Restoration Act, and he voted against linking the US and Israeli military (duh?). But on the other hand, within the last year he’s voted to approve $3.3 billion for Israel and $500 million for US-Israel missile defence cooperation. I can’t deny that, in many ways, Cleaver does right for the people of Kansas City. In regards to protecting healthcare, workers’ rights, or SNAP benefits, we can trust him to show up for us in DC.

Personally, I find myself torn between two conflicting desires: withholding my vote from a candidate who supports arming an apartheid state and adding my vote to a strong turnout for a seat the republicans tried to gerrymander away from us. The indignities and contradictions of politics under capitalism are endless.
Rick Brattin

is a current state senator. Leading up to the midterm, he’d raised $315k, the majority from individuals. The most recent FEC data show him a little over $457k, with the most recent donations from other conservative politicians and their PACs. A gerrymandered map was the only chance this guy had at getting elected.
Generally, this is a Lee’s Summit guy who was the auditor of Cass County and served four terms in MO house. He goes to the Christo-fascist Abundant Life Church, the megachurch that
sued jackson county
for “religious discrimination” during covid (case was settled with the county paying the church
of your dollars),
called same-sex relationships a “perversion
tried to take over the lee’s summit school board
to block the district’s
diversity efforts
, whose pastor testified in favor of a MO constitutional amendment to allow businesses to deny service to same-sex couples, and who held an “
a night for Israel"
event in 2024. Many of
his sponsored bills
show his willingness to inflict his own faith values on the general public.
Randy’s
the vice president of the Missouri Libertarian party but he’s really phoning it in. I think he just has a
personal facebook
where you wouldn’t even know he’s running for office.
The 6th district is currently held by Sam Graves, who announced earlier this year that he wouldn’t seek re-election. If you can’t tell from the map, this is a
rural, farming district
. In fact, it accounts for one third of Missouri’s state agriculture sales. It’s home to over 27,000 farms, of which 94% are family operations.
Josh Smead
is a father and architect living in Liberty.
His website

mentions his recent involvement in the Aloha Stadium Redevelopment Project in Honolulu, Hawai’i which is estimated to cost $350 million in taxpayer dollars. (It doesn’t appear that this project has been completed and it’s
significantly over budget

.) He’s raised the most of all the democratic nominees ($69k, all from individuals), but it’s still a fraction of some of the leading republicans in the race. His platform touches on a number of topics, but I notice that there’s nothing about military, war, technology, foreign aid, AI/data centers, ICE or federal police surveillance policies. If he’s worried that taking a stronger stance on these issues will alienate rural voters, I think he misunderstands the shared interests of the working class.
On a positive note
, he supports a congressional stock trading ban, supports five-year lobbying ban for former members of congress, and supports overturning citizens united.
Chris Stigall
is a conservative radio host.
This is a pretty good article summing up the republican primary dynamics:
Farm backing, Trump loyalty shape GOP race to replace Sam Graves in Missouri’s 6th Distric
t
Andy Maidment (L)
“Missouri’s independent watchdog agency.” Auditors make sure Missouri is using its public funds properly. Perform audits to ensure efficiency and compliance. They serve for four-year terms.
Quentin Wilson from Kirkwood, MO (near St. Louis), seems
well-qualified for the job

as a veteran of local, state and federal government. He’s been on the cabinet of democratic governors, served as deputy director of economic development, state commissioner of higher education, and director of the MO department of revenue. He has raised a little over $83k; $50k of that was a loan while the rest was all from individual donors.
Republican incumbent
Scott Fitzpatrick

was first elected in 2022, after having been appointed to the State Treasurer by governor Mike Parson. For some reason, he went into fundraising overdrive raising $413,777 from Missouri, California and Florida’s finest real estate developers, CEOs of investment agencies, presidents of private equity firms, bank CEOs, insurance PACs, attorneys and consultants. He also appears to have spent $3,103.44 of those dollars flying around on his taxpayer-funded private plane (see below).
Unlike Quentin Wilson, Fitzpatrick seems to be the
least qualified person

to determine responsible and ethical government spending. Less than one month after Fitzpatrick’s company “MariCorp” purchased an $800,000 aircraft, it applied for and received two federal Paycheck Protection Program loans totalling $1.3 million dollars. These were taxpayer-funded pandemic response loans intended to support small businesses by covering 8 weeks of their employee payroll costs. Taxpayers buying a 6-seat plane for this guy’s dock repair business? Not what I’d call proper or ethical use of public funds.
Fitzpatrick’s donors are the scourge of missouri monied interests: all six of
Steve Tilley’s pacs
are here (I’ve written about him in
past guides

), Fitzpatrick’s own pac “Missourians for a Responsible Budget” which was created to bypass individual campaign contribution limits, the PAC opposing amendment 5 called “Missourians Against Unfair Taxes”, and the Good Government Committee which created a Missouri Economic Development
office in Israel
to “promote mutually beneficial economic development opportunities”.
Dustin Coffell
is an accountant from the St. Louis area. And as far as Libertarians go, he may not be insufferable. His
campaign facebook

has posted memes about getting rid of Flock cameras. He’s called out politicians for their gerrymandering attempts. After the Supreme Court stayed the decisions, he wrote “It is my hope that this puts to rest any further attempts by the Secretary of State and Attorney General to subvert the referendum process enshrined in the Missouri constitution. The *people* run this state. Every elected official and candidate for public office should take note of that fact.”
Honestly, if you or your family members rightfully hate Scott Fitzpatrick but refuse to vote for a democrat, I encourage a vote for Dustin Coffell.

I can’t imagine anything worse than being a democrat in the Missouri state congress, and I’m convinced everyone on this ballot is a masochist. The job is essentially to listen to your constituents, be on committees, write bills, turn bills into laws (or don’t let bad bills turn into laws). If you’re a piece of shit, you use the position to make yourself and your friends some money, then move on to higher levels of power.

Incumbent Wick Thomas has done an incredible job in Jeff City - I trust them and am proud to have them represent me. Upon taking office, Wick became the first openly transgender or non-binary person elected to any state-level office in Missouri. In the last two years, they’ve sponsored
TWENTY ONE (!!) bills,

including ones for abolishing the death penalty, prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, supporting public and school libraries, and giving power back to local governments. The $28k they’ve raised this cycle has come from many individuals giving modest amounts.
This is Karen’s third attempt at this seat, and in November, it will be her third loss.
Uncontested

and I love her. Rep Young has been in office since 2019 (a special election to replace then-councilman Brandon Ellington). Her campaign has raised $56k from individuals, labor orgs and socially progressive PACS. She’s sponsored some
really great bills

that focus on the needs of children, families and seniors. She’s one of the pillars of the Ivanhoe Neighborhood and has transformed many of the vacant lots into greenspace and urban farms (she even has a regenerative farm in the neighborhood,
Young Family Farm KC
, whose produce can be found at Ivanhoe’s
saturday markets
Uncontested. This seat is currently held by Michael Johnson, who’s announced a run for city council (3rd in-district). What I like about Tony: he’s a board member for
Boys Grow

, he says his life’s mission is to “create quality affordable housing and equitable access to capital for families and professionals of color.” His linkedin says he’s an experienced litigator and former prosecutor, but his law website is now maybe an Indonesian gambling site? He has no campaign website or dedicated social media. He’s only received one campaign donation… ever ($500 from the Missouri Hospital Association). He uses his personal socials to share events and information from others. What I’m trying to get at is, Tony appears to have made no effort to make himself known to his future constituents, and I don’t like that. I hope he’s saving his energy for a positive Jeff City performance.
Another uncontested race in an office currently held by an aspiring city council member (Emily Weber, 4th at large).
Kevin Garner

has a ton of endorsements from labor unions and progressive orgs, which makes me optimistic about his inevitable tenure. He’s raised $117k from said orgs as well as many individual donors. Professionally, he’s the senior proposal strategist for federal government projects at burns and mcdonell and also served as the communications director for
Progress
Missouri.
He’s also the
co-founder
of the Midtown Democratic Club of Kansas City.
Pattie’s the incumbent and running uncontested. She was first elected in 2024, and has cosponsored
six bills
in her first term pertaining to education, healthcare services, expanding trauma center status for hospitals, and (my personal favorite)
a bill that prohibits AI developers

to advertising that their product is capable of providing therapy services or able to act as a mental health provider. Her campaign’s October MEC filings show $49k raised this election cycle, from individuals, labor pacs, and democratic orgs.

From the 2024 guide, she “served on the KCPS Board of Education for seven years (2014-2021) and has a career in non-profit work focused on health policy, public education and community engagement. The priorities of her campaign are access to health care, expanding childhood education and increasing resources for teachers and public schools, and pressing for fiscal policies and state programs that help families achieve self-sufficiency, maintain their rights to privacy in their healthcare decisions, and prioritize the well-being of children.”
Incumbent, uncontested. Since taking office in 2024, she has sponsored
sixteen (!) bills
. Some highlights include: eliminating the waiting week period for unemployment compensation, creating a criminal offense of “
masked intimidation

”, establishing a registry of persistent domestic violence offenders, and authorizing a sales tax exemption for supplies needed to care for infants. Her campaign fundraising has been limited this cycle, but I do see $1000 from Spire’s PAC.

From my 2024 write-up: Tiffany Price’s website says she’ll “champion evidence-based violence interruption and prevention initiatives that stop the cycle of harm before it starts.” The issues she wants to prioritize are health care (says it’s a human right, not a privilege), jobs, nondiscrimination, education, and reproductive rights. She’s the founder and executive director for Hold Em Up 4 Care whose mission is “to support equality for youth and adults by providing perfect-fit clothing, elevating self-esteem, and supporting mental health resilience with programs that directly improve their health and well-being”. And yeah Tiffany, now that you say it, I think a good bra is healthcare.
Incumbent, uncontested. Also elected in 2024,
Melissa Douglas
sponsored 9 bills in her first term. My
favorite bill

would create the “Success for Homeless and Foster Youth in Higher Education Act” which would require institutions of higher education to designate a homeless and foster student liaison in the financial aid office.

From the 2024 guide: “Melissa Douglas currently serves as the democratic party committee woman for the 17th ward. She doesn’t have a campaign website, but her linked in says she’s worked for KCPS for 15 years as a liaison for students/families  in transition or experiencing homelessness. Her flyers say that while in that position, she “developed and implemented KCPS Empowerment, a collective community impact program that provides positive solutions for at-risk students and homeless families.””

Donna Barnes is the incumbent, in a race against the same dude she beat in 2024. So, she shouldn’t have any trouble doing it again. She’s a retired postal worker and married to Jerome Barnes, who held the office before her. She sponsored
six bills
since taking office, and cosponsored around twenty. Honestly, none really stood out as particularly toothy or progressive, but I appreciated
one that would have established
a statewide communication access services program to improve resources for the deaf and hard of hearing in Missouri businesses and agencies.
Steven Hinton
is a batshit boomer from Raytown who uses his facebook to post AI slop, click bait, and engage in a
consummate tech struggle
This seat has been held for 8 years by democrat Keri Ingle. Now that she’s termed out, she’s aiming for the District 8 state senate seat (all hands on deck to help her win).
Michael Scott
is a pastor at an inclusive faith community, with a campaign tagline reading “
committed to community

”. His stated priorities include supporting public schools, supporting families (through empowering small businesses, fair wages, safe workplaces, affordable healthcare, paid family leave and workforce development), safe, thriving communities (with first-responder trainings, mental health resources, addiction recovery, and youth/neighborhood programs) and putting people first (ending gerrymandering, protecting citizen petition initiatives, and protecting the democratic process). His most recent campaign filings show about $34k in contributions, mostly from individuals with some labor and democratic PACs.
Jacquie’s

a funny one because she actually has pretty good politics. In interviews, she expressed an understanding of working class issues and had a lot of good ideas about how to address them (including expanding access to affordable healthcare, protecting social security and medicare). I think the only thing holding her back from identifying as a progressive are her antiquated beliefs around abortion and “traditional family values” (dogwhistle). She’s raised $31k this election. She has a PAC that seems to be created so she could receive $6k from the president of commercial real estate company, NorthPoint Development. It’s probably important to mention that NorthPoint development owns a number of downtown buildings and has built most of the new apartments on the Berkeley Riverfront (with a 15 year 75% tax exemption). Additionally, NorthPoint originally owned the land at the center of Independence’s data center battle. They sold it to the Dutch AI company, Nebius, who plans to build a four-building, $150 billion dollar data center that will be twice the size of Arrowhead Stadium. (Independence city council approved about $6.2 billion in tax breaks, forfeiting potential property tax revenue for the next 20 years.)
Another deja vu race from years prior.
Anthony Ealy
has held the seat since 2022 and has sponsored
23 bills

in that time. His bills address things like addiction and chronic disease, establish a yearly requirement for members of the Missouri generally assembly & parole board to visit department of corrections facilities and communicate with inmates, prohibiting state agencies from spending state funds on civil immigration detention, safe storage of firearms, and honestly many others that are worth reviewing.  Following ICE’s murder Renee Good, Ealy
reminded his neighbors
that they’re constitutionally allowed to record their interactions with federal immigration officers and encouraged them to do so if they see ICE activity in their area.
From my 2024 guide:

He’s an attorney at Ealy Law, Notary and Consulting, LLC and a former legislative fellow for US Rep Emanuel Cleaver. He’s also the youngest state representative in Missouri history as well as the first Black representative from Grandview. During law school, he had a 10-week summer fellowship working at the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades.”
Dave Thomas
has terrible politics, but they aren’t my main
beef
with him. This man has the audacity to disrespect Wendy’s founder and square patty innovator by using the domain “
truedavethomas.com

” for his personal website. The real Dave Thomas was a successful entrepreneur, unlike this imposter who is a low rung on an essential oil pyramid scheme. His book is free on amazon if you’re interested in the musings of someone potentially in religious psychosis.
Karissa Varga
doesn’t appear to have a campaign website, but her
Ballotpedia profile

has links to her personal facebook, instagram, youtube and linked in. Her facebook says she’s a nurse, and that she supports increasing access to health insurance, childcare, parental leave, affordability and food. Back in April, she joined the UAW machinists’ picketline who were striking for better contracts and wages. Her campaign has raised over $3k from individuals and local democrat politicians.

The County Executive acts as Jackson County's chief administrative officer. Imagine the county executive as the president or governor. The legislators write bills, vote on them and then the executive can pass or veto. And just as in the state or federal level, a vetoed bill can also be kicked back to the legislators to override. They have a large amount of administrative power that, until recently, has had seemingly little to no oversight.

The county legislators are responsible for all legislative duties in the County - introducing and enacting resolutions and ordinances, budget planning, etc. Voters in Jackson County will weigh in on six races: your one “in district” race, and each of the five “at large” races.
To read more about the candidates, I recommend these articles:
Jackson County Legislature is about to turn over. What candidates say on property taxes, stadiums, The Beacon
Stacy Lake’s

background is really impressive; she studied finance at UMKC, moved to Beijing to study Chinese language, then got her law degree. She’s been an attorney in KC for over 11 years, including an internship at the jackson county prosecutor’s office. I actually
learn a lot
about her from
her posts in the r/kansascity
reddit page. Her
“JACKSON” 7 point plan

promises: justice system reform (preventing crime through technology/911 investment, economic opportunities/ban the box measures, etc.), audit jackson county government, county-wide infrastructure (including ADA compliance), keeping taxes affordable, small business support, ownership and affordable housing, and a neighbor-to-neighbor transportation plan (investing in bus lines and bike/pedestrian safety). According to the
survey answers

, she does not believe in continued expansion of AI data centers in Jackson County and would rather focus on modernizing our own infrastructure and bringing in industries that promote economic growth. I know people who are skeptical about Lake as an aspiring career politician, but I think that’s only a drawback if they’re willing to make concessions to money or power (something she hasn’t shown us, so far).

Stacy has raised almost $107k this election cycle from individuals, labor pacs and progressive orgs. She’s endorsed by AFL-CIO, the local transit union, SEIU, firefighters and teachers, as well as Abortion Action MO.
Alan Rohlfing
retired from the Army and began a career in workforce development, particularly employment and entrepreneurship training for vets and active military members.
He’s running for

more transparent assessments and a simpler appeals process. Wants to reduce government spending and support first responders. He’s raised just over $13k this election, most from individuals with a couple republican pacs chipping in.
Kelly Thompson

has been active in Kansas City for a while, particularly as a mom to kids in the KC public schools. A quote from her website says that “Our leaders should be grounded in service to the community, focused on building systems that truly support all of us, and work for people with clarity, purpose, and accountability.” She ran a good campaign for school board in 2025, but lost to the incumbent. She’s raised more than most candidates running for Jackson County legislature ($30k), with support from individuals, labor unions, and notable democrats/democratic orgs. You can see a full list of her endorsements on her
ballotpedia page.

I believe Kelly and I share a lot of the same politics, but I have one concern. When I was doing research for the 2025 school board election, I noted that she was the director of client services at Evertune AI. Currently,
her linked in

says she’s a “human-centered design & innovation strategist” (what are we even doing, people) at a company called Together Works. There’s no mention of Evertune AI on the experience portion of her linked in, and it just feels like she’s downplaying the whole “working in the AI sector” throughout her campaign. We’ll need legislators that won’t sell out Jackson County to data centers and won’t push to incorporate AI technologies across the county. I hope that we can count on her in that regard.
Venessa Huskey

is the incumbent, she ran in 2022 against a couple other dems in the primary and unopposed in the november election. She’s a retired Program Analyst for the Bureau of Fiscal Services, and has been active in her neighborhood and a volunteer for
many arts programs
in KC. She’s raised $2,500, all from three labor PACs: building and construction trades, iron workers, and roofers.
Phyllis Hernandez
has spent time in Jeff City as a legislative aid to progressive democrats. She’s an artist and muralist who owns and operates her own gallery, Sala de Arte. She sits on the board of
Northeast Arts KC
and Guadalupe Center charter school, and is a member of the mayor’s
small business task force

. It appears her campaign didn’t file any MEC reports until after the midterms, but it looks like she’s raised $1,275 this cycle; $500 from the KC regional association of realtors and the rest from individuals.
Scott Qualls
is the facilities coordinator at the women and family center of City Union Mission. For someone who has such daily proximity to people experiencing homelessness and desperate situations,
he’s focused
more on punitive reactions to crime (stronger police force and investing in detention facilities) than preventive measures. He’s raised $6.5k, seemingly all from individual donors.
Byron Townsend

is currently an at-large member of the Hickman Mills board of education and retired after 30 years of carrying letters in Kansas City. During Townsend’s tenure, the former superintendent of the school district, Yaw Obeng, was abruptly fired as the district faced allegations of financial mismanagement and improper activity. Obeng has recently filed a lawsuit against the district alleging that board president Bonnaye Mims “refused to speak directly to Obeng once her term began, and that she told him in early 2025 -- in front of other board members — that she had been declining to speak to him on the basis of his Ghanaian ancestry and Canadian nationality.” From the
July 10th KC Star article
“The lawsuit further alleges that Mims said Obeng’s ethnic and national identity prevented him from understanding “how we do things,” and alleges that board member
Byron Townsend
voiced his agreement at the time. The lawsuit alleges that these statements were repeated and escalated over time by multiple board members, with some allegedly telling Obeng to ‘go back to Africa.’”

Despite this, Townsend’s endorsed by five local unions, freedom inc, southland progress, and trusted democratic state representatives. Prior to the midterm, he’d raised around $2k from individuals. I think the labor unions must’ve been holding out to see who got the nomination, because his latest MEC filings report $12k. His
four district priorities
are fair and honest property tax assessments, accountability in county government, lower bills for working families, and to be a “neighbor, not insider”.
Republican challenger
Lon McDonald

doesn’t have much information on his website besides a bio and a map of the district. His tagline seems to be “property tax, transparency, fiscal responsibility.” He’s currently a Jackson County councilman to the University of Missouri extension and is the founder of Textile Care Group, an upholstery cleaning company. He shared one anti-flock-camera post on facebook, but is also sharing misinformation about amendment 6.

I think it’s possible this race could be close? McDonald was unopposed in the primary and received 1,083 votes. Townsend and his democratic challenger had a combined 12,551 votes. Townsend’s school district stuff is concerning, and we don’t ultimately know (from the article) the specifics of his behavior.
Tony Lawson a professional historian and the director of the Downtown Blue Springs Community Improvement District. He and his wife own the Bean Counter Cafe. I found some
old blog posts
he wrote

back in 2014 when he was a graduate student at UMKC, and I find them very endearing. I wish every politician had his passion for/understanding of Kansas City history, because it makes for much more effective governing in the present.
Bill Haley
is another candidate running to reform the assessment process. As the owner of an ammunition store, it’s no surprise that public safety is his “foundational” issue.
His website

is funny because whoever built it gave Bill some writing prompts to provide more specificity around his priorities, but he just left the prompts in. In 2024, he was elected to the Lee’s Summit Board of Education.
Litigation attorney
Carla Fields

is a partner at Fields & Brown, LLC, the oldest and largest minority-owned law firm in Kansas City. She’s been active in the Jackson County Bar Association and the Hickman Mills School District. According to
her website

, her priorities are accountable leadership, safer communities, affordable living, and economic growth. But frankly, I don’t see much detail explaining how she plans to execute those priorities. Her campaign has raised $7k, all from individuals. Defense attorney that defends the school.
Lance Pollard
lives in Grain Valley and owns a plumbing business. Like many of his peers,
he’s focused on providing
more accountability in the assessment process. He’s raised about $21k, and has
promised to donate
100% of his legislative salary to “local nonprofit organizations and community advocates”.
Incumbent
Donna Peyton
has served one term in the legislature, where she’s the chair of two committees: Budget and Housing & Homelessness.
In the last four years

, co-sponsored legislation that supported social services programming, including the creation of a Senior Services Fund. She’s also been our best champion for regional transit. Prior to her role in Jackson County, she was on the Raytown School Board. She’s endorsed by multiple political orgs and labor unions, and has raised just over $7.5k from individuals, the AFL-CIO, local 124, and the greater KC building and construction trades.
Some of you may remember
Gresia Cabrera
from her run for city council in the 4th district. (In 2023, she was running as Grace Cabrera.) Here’s what I wrote about her then:

“Grace Cabrera isn’t a serious candidate, she just seems to be using her family’s history as Cuban anti-communists to capitalize on the current red scare within the far-right (and nation, at large). Her priorities are backwards and her talking points demonstrate a fundamental misunderstanding of the US’s long history of systematic racism, oppression, and exploitation.” She’ll make it through this primary, but I’m comforted to know that she’ll lose in November.
Her website
outlines her priorities. She’s raised $3.5k from individuals and the conservative Jackson County Liberty PAC.
Former UMKC Vice Chancellor for diversity and inclusion (2014-2021), COMBAT Commissioner, she’s
been involved

in tons of orgs including Swope Health Services, St. Luke’s, the Statewide African American Mental Health Taskforce, and Healthcare Foundation of Greater KC. She’s raised $27k from mostly individuals. There was one weird in-kind donation from “Pete AI agent”, which appears to be provided by a local tech group that made
her website
. I think just have a human make your campaign site next time.

Each state plus D.C. has at least one Supreme Court. The Supreme Courts do not hear trials of cases. They hear appeals of the decisions made in the lower trial or appellate courts. The judges who control these seats are elected by the public.

Appointed to the Supreme Court in 2012. He cast a favorable vote in the gerrymandering debacle and wrote the majority opinion on abortion access (i.e., his rulings were favorable if you are against the gerrymandered map and for abortion access).

title: Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District

children.text: The Missouri Court of Appeals is an intermediate appellate court, which serves as an intermediate step between the trial courts and the courts of last resort in a state. From the Missouri Court of Appeals
ballotpedia

page: “Based on the number of counties in its jurisdiction (45), the Western District is the state's largest intermediate appellate court, and is located in its own courthouse in downtown Kansas City. The court is composed of 11 judges and handles almost 40 percent of the appellate caseload in Missouri.”

One case that helped me decide to retain Judge Hardwick was “R.M.A., Appellant, v. BLUE SPRINGS IV SCHOOL DISTRICT (2024).” Here’s the gist: a transgender student in the Blue Springs school district wanted to use a particular bathroom but the school refused. The student filed sex-based discrimination, as they were denied equal public accommodations. The Missouri Supreme Court substantiated the claim, the case went to trial, and the jury ruled in the student’s favor, saying the school district needed to pay $4.2 million in damages.

The case would then go through years of overturning and appeals, between circuit courts, appellate courts and the Missouri Supreme Court. Ultimately, the student lost the case over a decade after they initially filed. But when it was in Judge Hardwick’s court, she voted in favor of the student and, as I see it, in a way that correctly interprets the law.

It’s important to remember that this is a ladder that (it’s safe to assume) most judges want to climb up ultimately toward the Missouri Supreme Court or federal appointment. Whatever gatekeeping is employed at the lowest levels ultimately gets replicated as they move through their careers. The people we grant power to within our local courts eventually will be the same people who accumulate greater and greater power within our state and, possibly, country.
In Missouri, a judicial circuit can encompass one or more counties (see
Missouri Circuit Courts

). Each circuit court can have several divisions, including circuit, associate, small claims, probate, family, or drug court. Each division hears cases within its particular area of subject-matter jurisdiction, and jurisdiction is based on the size or type of a civil claim or the severity or type of a criminal charge. Drug court, for example, hears only drug-related criminal cases.

Appointed in 2013 by Jay Nixon (D), prior to that an associate circuit judge in Jackson County, assistant prosecuting attorney and an assistant attorney general. From a performance review survey completed by his staff: “I wish we had more judges like Judge Garrett. He’s concerned about staff; that they have the proper tools and training for their jobs. He’s always willing to help others. He makes all staff feel appreciated to make them know that what they do is important. He addresses all court staff with respect and is always willing to shake hands and tell us ‘thank you’”. The judicial performance review committee recommends he be retained; you can read their evaluation
here

Appointed by Gov. Mike Parson in 2024. Prior to appointment, he was an assistant US attorney for the western district and assistant prosecuting attorney for Jackson County. I have been told that Judge Edwards is fair in his rulings, listens to arguments, and has competent responses. The judicial performance review committee recommends he be retained; you can read their evaluation
here

I got very sincere, positive feedback about Judge Barett. I was told that she is a good person who “really wants to get it right”. Judge Barrett was appointed in 2024, and prior to that she served as Associate Circuit Judge of Division 30 for the 16th Judicial Circuit Court from July 2023-September 2024, was Chief Trial Assistant for the Jackson County Prosecutor’s Office, and was an Assistant Attorney General for the Missouri Attorney General’s Office. The judicial performance review committee recommends she be retained; you can read their evaluation
here

Corey Atkins was the Jackson County circuit judge who overturned the jury’s verdict that awarded damages to the Blue Springs student. A trusted source warned me that Judge Atkins comes from an extremely conservative family, and he did not fall far from the tree – socially and fiscally. I was also informed that public defenders do not like Judge Atkins. He worked for the attorney general’s office (state prosecutors) before being a clerk for Zel Fischer (most conservative judge on the Missouri Supreme Court). He does not have a reputation for sympathy toward defendants in terms of ROR bonds. The judicial performance review committee recommends retention, but he received some of the lowest scores I’ve seen from the
lawyer survey.

Judge Harrell was described to me as balanced and fair during jury selection and trial. An attorney told me that he’s a good judge overall. He was appointed in 2012 and has served as Presiding Judge. Prior to this appointment, he was an Administrative Family Court judge and chief deputy prosecuting attorney for the Jackson County Prosecutor’s office.

One anecdote: Kansas City has the Urban Homesteading program that gives vacant or abandoned homes to neighbors who are able to bring them up to code and live in them once restored. This relies on utilizing the abandoned housing act. Some judges get scared of these cases, but Harrell, who appreciates and understands the program, has taken the cases enthusiastically. The only negative I heard is that he doesn’t appreciate the difficulty in litigating civil rights work. The judicial performance review committee recommends he be retained; you can read their evaluation
here

Judge Rothermitch was appointed in 2023 and was given a special assignment “Criminal A Rotation” in 2025. She comes from the attorney general’s office, where she was deputy chief of employment litigation and an assistant attorney general before that. She also spent six years at Legal Aid of Western Missouri. She was described to me as an “amazing attorney” and “fair” (despite the attorney general’s office being a pretty negative origin story). She is supportive of defendants’ attorney’s arguments in eviction and debt defense court. The judicial performance review committee recommends she be retained; you can read their evaluation
here
Appointed by Mike Parson in 2019. Willingham often presides over debt collection cases, including people being sued over
unpaid medical bills

. It’s been shared with me that Judge Willingham makes unfair judgments and is majorly biased towards landlords. Another said he listens seriously to arguments in the collections dockets. There are some very clear examples of Judge Willingham harming tenants and blatantly misunderstanding the law, including evicting a disabled long-term tenant from public housing for having a medical marijuana card prescription (no evidence of using or even possession). He also does strong man competitions (derogatory) and is a member of the fucking Federalist Society.

In 2022, I wrote “Right off the top, this guy looks like someone who just filmed an angry rant from the driver's seat of his Ford F150.” Not only will I stand by that assessment, I’ll raise it and say he seems like a guy who would openly say white guys can’t get a fair shake these days. The review committee does recommend retention, you can read it
here
. In my opinion, this is THE ONE we need to get out of the courts.

Judge Bird-Riley was appointed in 2020. Prior to appointment, she was a Family Court Commissioner in the 16th circuit, and has also worked in private practice firms. Multiple sources providing extremely positive remarks about Judge Bird-Riley. They describe her as very defendant friendly in eviction court, as well as fair and considered in her decisions. The judicial performance review committee recommends retention, read their review
here

Appointed in 2013, Judge Weir presides over the criminal domestic violence diversion docket for all domestic violence diversion cases in the county. Prior to appointment, she was an attorney for the Missouri state public defender system and then as a contract attorney representing survivors of domestic violence and their children in Family Court. Judge Weir was described to me as the most fair and experienced judge on the landlord-tenant court and is defendant-friendly in debt-collection court. Of the judges in eviction court, she is the most tenant-friendly. She promotes the Right to Counsel in her courtroom and is willing to extend cases when tenants are waiting on rental assistance. Seems more lenient and willing to listen to a tenant than the others.
The judicial performance review committee recommends she be retained, you can read the review
here

title: Amendments to the Missouri State Constitution

children.text: “Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to:
Repeal the 2024 voter-approved Amendment providing reproductive healthcare rights, including abortion through fetal viability;
Allow abortions for rape and incest (under twelve weeks’ gestation), emergencies, and fetal anomalies;
Allow legislation regulating abortion;
Ensure parental consent for minors’ abortions;
Prohibit gender transition procedures for minors?”
This bill reverses reproductive rights we JUST passed in 2024. And this time, there are added restrictions that give lawmakers broad authority to create new regulations around our healthcare.

As you may have noticed by the signs, the conservatives backing this ballot measure have shifted their messaging away from abortion and towards demonizing children. Gender-affirming surgeries for minors have been
banned in Missour
i since 2023, as are puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones.

But even before 2023, the surgeries were rare. An internal Washington University review found its transgender center stopped referring minors for surgery in late 2018. Six chest surgeries were performed by university physicians on adolescents transitioning to male between 2018 and 2023, but the referrals came from outside providers. A
2024 study
from Harvard found no gender-affirming surgery performed on transgender youths ages 12 or younger, anywhere in the US.

Regardless, The American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Medical Association support gender-affirming care for transgender youth. We know that when young people receive even non-surgical gender affirming care (like social affirmation, name or pronoun changes, therapy, or reversible puberty delaying medication for teens), it can be lifesaving in mitigating negative mental health outcomes such as depression, anxiety, and suicidality. Here are six studies that support those claims:
Tordoff, et al. 2022
Turban & Ehrensaft 2017
Dolotina & Turban 2022
Olsavsky et al. 2023
Branstrom & Pachankis 2020
Kuper et al. 2020

.  The messaging behind this campaign seeks to address a problem that doesn’t exist. It’s rooted in a bias against transgender identities and ultimately harms and stigmatizes the children they claim to want to protect.

The facts are these: Most Missouri voters want abortion access, we already won this at the ballot. A HELL NO on Amendment 3 protects that access and the ban on gender-affirming surgeries for young people remains the same.

Sponsors: all male republican representatives Ed Lewis, John Simmons, Bill Irwin, Michael Davis, Christopher Warwick, Alex Riley, Ben Baker, Matthew Overcast, Bennie Cook. Missouri Catholic Conference, Missouri Right to Life, and Priests for Life.
Two campaign committees in support: Her Health, Her Future PAC (whose treasurer is Claudia Kehoe, wife to the Missouri Governor) and Missouri Right to Life PAC
“Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to:
Expand the initiative and referendum petition process by making it a fundamental right;
Allow courts to revise ballot summaries through lawsuits;
Prohibit the legislature from weakening initiative or referendum powers;

Prohibit the legislature from changing or repealing laws enacting through the initiative process, or passing laws similar to those rejected by referendum, without approval from at least 80% of both chambers; and
Preserve existing majority vote and signature requirements for initiative and referendum petitions?”

If Amendment 6 passes, Jeff City legislators would need 80% of both the House and Senate to change state laws enacted through the citizen initiative process. As it stands (and as we’ve seen on many occasions), our lawmakers can amend or repeal voter-approved constitutional amendments with a simple majority of the house and senate. (Republicans have controlled the Missouri house and senate since 2003.)
A Yes on 6 would also enshrine the initiative and referendum as a “fundamental right” and prohibit lawmakers from weakening the process. It would also require ballot language to be clear and fair.

We have spent two decades watching our hard-won laws be overturned, overridden and undermined by republicans. Widely-supported citizen initiatives like the right to reproductive freedom (2024), Medicaid expansion (2020), limits to campaign contributions, lobbying and legislative gifts (2018) have been completely eliminated or drastically weakened by our elected officials.

Respect MO Voters is leading the campaign with the support of multiple unions and statewide organizing groups like the Missouri Sierra Club, Veterans for All Voters, Missouri Congregations United, and the NAACP.

Leading the opposition is republican Joe Niccola, state senator from District 11 which includes Independence, Sugar Creek, and parts of Grain Valley and Oak Grove. I’ll say it’s an interesting gambit to go so hard against a measure meant to protect the will of the people you profess to serve.

“Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to establish a permanent public endowment fund to support state government instead of taxing Missouri residents, prohibit the General Assembly from appropriating or diverting the fund, and eliminate the state-imposed taxes once the fund generates sufficient revenue to replace them?”

This is a long-con to eliminate state taxes in the most wiley coyote ACME products ass scheme. This would be accomplished, they propose, by creating a permanent state investment fund and replacing that revenue with investment earnings from the fund. In other words, letting the interest earned from this pot replace our state tax earnings. The thing is, Missouri generates over $18 billion each year in tax revenue. So, in order for the fund to generate the interest capable of eliminating our taxes, this fund would need to grow to
at least $600 billion

As a concept, these types of state investment funds aren’t particularly novel, but they’re almost always funded by some “bonus” money, whether that’s the state winning a settlement, an operating surplus, leftover federal funds, a surprise diamond mine, idk. The geniuses behind Amendment 7’s plan have no dedicated funding source. Which means they’re going to use our tax dollars, diverting them from things we actually need like education, healthcare, senior services, or affordable housing at a time when critical services are already being slashed by $2 billion.
At the rate they’re proposing to fund the pot, it’s estimated that it could take as long as one hundred years for the fund to pay anything back. (The sponsor of the bill even
admits it.

) What’s even more concerning is that once the money is put into the fund, the state cannot withdraw any revenue until taxes are eliminated. So all we’re doing is taking money away from today’s much-needed services on a gamble that may or may not start paying off until the year 2150. It’s a bad investment.

This was a bill introduced during the legislative session by republican state Senator Adam Schnelting from St. Charles. It was passed by the house and senate, so now it’s on the ballot. Schnelting’s other jobs include: licensed realtor, minister and former church planter.

“Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to support law enforcement by preserving the right of citizens to elect a county sheriff, prohibiting the removal of a county sheriff except by a writ of quo warranto, and recognizing the office of sheriff as part of the administration of justice.”

This measure would make sheriffs nearly impossible to remove. Under the current system, bad sheriffs can be removed through the local courts. If passed, Amendment 8 would make it so only the state attorney general could initiate the process of removal. We also already elect our sheriff, so nothing changes in that aspect.

This was a bill introduced during the legislative session by republican state senator Jill Carter and republican state rep Bennie Cook. It was passed by the house and senate, so now it’s on the ballot.

“Do the people of the state of Missouri approve the act of the General Assembly entitled “house Bill No. 1 (2025 Second Extraordinary Session),” which repeals Missouri’s existing congressional plan and replaces it with new congressional boundaries that keep more counties intact?”

Don’t let the wording of this bill fool you: keeping “counties intact” would mean breaking our community apart. If we don’t defeat prop A, we will be subjected to the republican’s gerrymandered congressional map we saw during the midterms. You can read all about it
in my last guide

, but Kansas City’s democratic stronghold will be broken into three districts where our votes will be diluted. Missouri will lose one of its two democratic House Representatives in DC. My neighborhood in the Historic Northeast will vote with rural constituents living at the Iowa/Illinois border. To illustrate how bizarre the gerrymandered map is, the Kansas City University campus on Independence Avenue would have buildings in the 5th and 6th district and one parking lot in the 4th.
Mark fucking Alford and Denny bitchass Hoskins.

“Shall Jackson County continue its anti-crime sales tax, commonly known as COMBAT, at the rate of one-quarter of one cent for a period of ten years for the purpose of promoting and providing public safety with Jackson County, including the prevention and treatment of drug abuse and addiction and the prevention, investigation, prosecution and detention of violent criminals and drug dealers? The proceeds of this tax shall be deposited in a special Jackson County Anti-Crime Sales Tax Trust Fund, separate from the general fund or any other county funds.”

The Community Backed Anti-Crime Tax (COMBAT) dates back to 1989. It was dedicated to “combating” substance abuse and drug related crime, then expanded its mission in 2009 to reducing violence of any kind (not just drug-related). It generates approximately $25-$30 million per year. About 60% of the funds go towards courts and law enforcement agencies, namely drug court and the jackson county drug task force. The other 40% is distributed as grants to violence prevention and treatment programs. Recipients of COMBAT funding include Cornerstones of Care which provides family therapy, and the Metropolitan Organization Countering Sexual Assault. The COMBAT website is really informative and, in my opinion, refreshingly transparent. Read more about the programs they support
here
It’s it perfect? No. But it’s the best we have right now, and certainly better than leaving it up to the cops.
No one, the tax is extended 10 years at a time.
